newsitem.title: USA: Securitek former president pleads guilty.
newsitem.headline: Securitek former president pleads guilty.

text.p: The former president of a security and surveillance company that traded its stock over the counter has pleaded guilty to a scheme to defraud customers of a New York brokerage firm, prosecutors said on Friday.

The man, Bertram Slutsky, a former president of Securitek International Corp, was accused in a federal two-count Information with conspiracy to commit securities and wire fraud and interstate promotion of commercial bribery.
Securitek, formerly called U.S. Asset Corp, designs and markets security and surveillance systems for the military, government and law enforcement agencies.
Slutsky entered his guilty plea on Thursday in Manhattan federal court.
Slutsky is also alleged to have owned or controlled a majority of the outstanding common stock of Securitek.
The charges stem from an FBI sting operation in which agents posed as corrupt brokers willing to accept bribes for selling stock to their customers.

In entering his plea, Slutsky admitted that in late 1995 he entered into an unlawful agreement with Jeffrey Szur, the owner of J.S. Securities, Inc., a broker-dealer registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
According to the charges, Szur and Slutsky recruited several others to operate four J.S. Securities branch offices to solicit more customers to buy Securitek stock.

The two men agreed that Slutsky would pay their co-conspirators between 35 and 50 percent of the proceeds of such sales of Securitek stock with the understanding that these payments would not be disclosed to customers.
As a result of using high-pressure sales tactics, prosecutors allege that the brokerage sold more than 1.8 million shares of Securitek common stock.

A 29-count indictment unsealed in New York on Tuesday charged Szur, his mother and four others, who worked as supervisors for the brokerage with conspiracy, wire fraud, bribery, falsifying records and money laundering in connection with a scheme with Slutsky.

At his plea before U.S. District Judge John Koeltl, Slutsky said he agreed with others, including Szur, to violate the securities laws by making payments to brokers from the proceeds of sales of Securitek stock.

He also admitted that he knew the brokers were involved in alleged violations of their fiduciary duties to customers by not disclosing their receipt of the money and that customers allegedly were being defrauded.
Slutsky faces up to 15 years in prison and at least $1.25 million in fines when sentenced in November.
